funFacts: Built like English week-end and German Wochenende — but in Arabic order: “end (of) the week”.

etymology.text: Wiktionary: inherited from Proto-Semitic *yawm-. Plural أَيَّام.

funFacts: Hebrew יוֹם (yom) is the same word.
الْيَوْمَ, “today”, is simply “the day” in the accusative.
pitfalls: Plural أَيَّام; after 3–10 the genitive plural: ثَلَاثَةُ أَيَّامٍ (a masculine noun takes the number with ة).
الْيَوْمُ (-u: the day, today as subject: الْيَوْمُ الْأَحَدُ) vs الْيَوْمَ (-a: the adverb “today”).
subtleties: يَوْمَ + day name, with no preposition, means “on”: يَوْمَ السَّبْتِ = on Saturday.

etymology.text: Wiktionary: from Proto-Semitic *laylay-; it can be analysed as a singulative of لَيْل (night-time) + ـَة. Cognates: Classical Syriac lēlyā, Aramaic lēləyā, Hebrew לַיְלָה (láyla).

اللَّيْلَةَ (adverb) is “tonight”, not “the night” in general (that is اللَّيْلُ).
subtleties: One night = لَيْلَةٌ; at night (in general) = فِي اللَّيْلِ or لَيْلًا.

Times of day are named after the prayers: الْفَجْرُ (dawn), الظُّهْرُ (noon), الْعَصْرُ (afternoon), الْمَغْرِبُ (sunset), الْعِشَاءُ (night).

funFacts: Hebrew הַיּוֹם (hayom), “the day”, is built the same way; Greek σήμερα and German heute also come from “this day”.
pitfalls: الْيَوْمَ (-a) is the adverb; الْيَوْمُ (-u) is “the day” as a subject: الْيَوْمُ الْأَحَدُ (today is Sunday).
subtleties: It can stand at the start or at the end: الْيَوْمَ أَعْمَلُ = أَعْمَلُ الْيَوْمَ.

profile.feeling: Plans and promises.

examples.tr: We’ll meet tomorrow at the café.

phrases.tr: tomorrow is near for the one who watches for it
phrases.meaning: what you wait for will come soon; time will tell

synonyms.nuance: tomorrow — the spoken word in the Levant and Egypt

etymology.text: Wiktionary: the adverbial accusative of غَد (ġad, “morrow; tomorrow”, a noun).

funFacts: بَعْدَ غَدٍ is “the day after tomorrow”.
pitfalls: غَدًا is the adverb; the noun is غَد: بَعْدَ غَدٍ, الْغَدُ (the morrow).
subtleties: The present tense with غَدًا already means the future: أُسَافِرُ غَدًا = I’m travelling tomorrow.

derivedFrom.none: a basic word, not made from another

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

profile.feeling: What just happened.

examples.text: كَانَتْ قَرْيَةً صَغِيرَةً بِالْأَمْسِ، وَهِيَ الْيَوْمَ مَدِينَةٌ كَبِيرَةٌ.
examples.tr: Only yesterday it was a small village; today it is a big city.

synonyms.nuance: yesterday, last night — and the source of the spoken مبارح (Levant)

etymology.text: Wiktionary: from Proto-Semitic *ʔamšay- (“yesterday”); cognate with Akkadian amšālim. Compare Hebrew אֶמֶשׁ (last night).

funFacts: Hebrew אֶמֶשׁ (emesh, last night) is a cousin.
pitfalls: أَمْسِ ends in -i and never changes; with the article it is a noun: الْأَمْسُ, بِالْأَمْسِ.
subtleties: With yesterday the verb is in the past (lesson C01); “was” is كَانَ: كُنْتُ, كَانَ.

profile.feeling: Right now, this moment.

etymology.text: Wiktionary: the definite accusative of آن (ʾān, “time”).

funFacts: Literally “the time” — like Greek τώρα, a word for a moment of time.
pitfalls: Always with al- and -a: الْآنَ (al-ʾāna), never *آنَ alone.
subtleties: Often at the end: أَنَا مَشْغُولٌ الْآنَ (I’m busy now).

profile.feeling: Not now — afterwards.

etymology.text: The accusative of لَاحِق (“following, subsequent”), the active participle of لَحِقَ (“to catch up with”) (Wiktionary: لَاحِق).

funFacts: Its root means “to follow, to catch up”: later is what follows.
pitfalls: Not “late”: لَاحِقًا = afterwards; late = مُتَأَخِّرًا.
subtleties: أَرَاكَ لَاحِقًا (lesson 2) is a fixed goodbye.

profile.feeling: Anticipation: it will happen soon.

examples.tr: I’ll be back soon — wait for me.

etymology.text: Wiktionary: an adverb; compare قَرُبَ (“to be near”) — the accusative of قَرِيب (near, lesson 12).

funFacts: Near in space and soon in time are one root: قَرِيب.
pitfalls: قَرِيبٌ (adjective: near) agrees with its noun; قَرِيبًا (adverb: soon) never changes.
subtleties: Greek has two words (σύντομα / κοντά); Arabic uses one form for “soon” and “nearby”.

profile.feeling: Alarm clocks and empty streets.

examples.tr: My father leaves the house early.

etymology.text: Wiktionary: the adverbial accusative of مُبَكِّر (“early”), the active participle of بَكَّرَ; root ب ك ر.

funFacts: The same root gives بِكْر (first-born) and بُكْرَة (early morning — and the spoken word for “tomorrow”).
pitfalls: The k is doubled: mubakkiran.
subtleties: As an adjective it agrees: الْقِطَارُ مُبَكِّرٌ (the train is early).

override.meaning: Wiktionary lists مُتَأَخِّرًا only as the accusative of مُتَأَخِّر, which it glosses “late; delayed”.

profile.feeling: Apologies and missed buses.

etymology.text: The accusative of مُتَأَخِّر (“late, delayed”), the active participle of تَأَخَّرَ (“to be late, to remain behind”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Its root ء خ ر is in آخِر (last) and أَخِيرًا (finally).
pitfalls: Not مُؤَخَّرًا, which means “recently, lately”.
subtleties: As an adjective it agrees: الْحَافِلَةُ مُتَأَخِّرَةٌ (the bus is late); as an adverb it stays مُتَأَخِّرًا.

profile.feeling: Habits that never change.

examples.tr: I always drink coffee in the morning.

etymology.text: Wiktionary: the adverbial accusative of دَائِم (“lasting, enduring”); root د و م.

funFacts: The same root gives دَوَام, working hours: دَوَامٌ كَامِلٌ = full-time.
pitfalls: The hamza sits on a yāʾ seat: دَائِمًا (dāʾiman).
subtleties: It can stand before the verb or at the end of the sentence.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

contrasts.value: the adverb كَثِيرًا as a word of its own (often, a lot)

profile.feeling: Many times — and a lot.

examples.tr: We often travel in the summer.

etymology.text: Wiktionary: from the root ك ث ر — the adverbial accusative of كَثِير (“many”, lesson 5).

funFacts: The same form كَثِيرًا is also the accusative of the adjective كَثِير (lesson 5).
pitfalls: كَثِيرًا مَا + verb = “often”: here مَا is not a negation.
subtleties: After a verb it can mean “a lot” or “often”: أَقْرَأُ كَثِيرًا.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

profile.feeling: What happens most of the time.

examples.tr: I usually go to work by bus.

collocations.tr: it is usually the case that …

etymology.text: The accusative of غَالِب (“predominant, preponderant”), the active participle of غَلَبَ (“to overcome”) (Wiktionary: غَالِب).

funFacts: From “to prevail”: what prevails is what usually happens; أَغْلَبِيَّة is a majority.
pitfalls: It also means “probably”: هُوَ غَالِبًا فِي الْبَيْتِ = he’s probably at home.
subtleties: A scale: دَائِمًا (always) – غَالِبًا (usually) – كَثِيرًا (often) – أَحْيَانًا (sometimes) – لَا … أَبَدًا (never).

features.derivedFrom: أَحْيَان (times, plural of حِين), in the accusative

profile.feeling: Now and then.

examples.tr: We sometimes go to the restaurant.

synonyms.nuance: sometimes (lit. in some of the times)

etymology.text: Wiktionary: the adverbial accusative of أَحْيَان (“times”), the plural of حِين (time).

funFacts: Literally “at times” — exactly the English expression.
pitfalls: A plural noun used as an adverb: أَحْيَانًا (not *حِينًا) for “sometimes”.
subtleties: It can open the sentence (أَحْيَانًا أَعْمَلُ لَيْلًا) or close it.
